statements.quote: Every model in this course contains two kinds of numbers: **parameters**, which *learning* changes, and **hyperparameters**, which *you choose* before learning starts.
This chapter is about the second kind: what it is, why it cannot be solved for, and how practitioners actually find good values.
A **parameter** is a quantity the training algorithm updates.
The weights $W$ of a transformer are parameters: they start at random values and are moved by gradient descent until the [loss](losslab.php) stops decreasing.
A model may have billions of them, and you never pick one by hand.
A **hyperparameter** is a quantity that stays *fixed* during training and is *chosen* by the practitioner before it starts.
It sits outside the learned weights and determines what the model is and how it is trained:
| Category | Hyperparameter | Chosen as |
| Architecture | $d_{\text{model}}$, $N$ layers, $h$ heads, FFN width, context size, vocabulary size | integers, often constrained ($d_{\text{model}}$ a multiple of $h$) |
| Optimization | learning rate, optimizer (SGD / Adam / …), batch size, number of epochs, weight decay | continuous (learning rate usually on a log scale) or categorical |
| Data | context length, tokenization scheme, data mixing | integers / categorical |
| Inference | temperature, top-$p$ | continuous (see the [Temperature & Sampling](samplinglab.php) chapter) |

You have already set several of these: the learning rate and optimizer in the [Optimizer chapter](optimizerlab.php), $d_{\text{model}}$, $h$, $N$ and context size in the [Transformer chapter](transformer.php).
The boundary is not perfectly clean.

A learning-rate *schedule* is a function you choose whose value changes over time, and every optimizer carries its own hyperparameters (Adam's $\beta_1$, $\beta_2$, $\epsilon$), so choices nest inside other choices.
The `optimizer` slot itself hides a sub-family of choices.

The names you have seen in the [Optimizer chapter](optimizerlab.php) — SGD and Adam — are just two of about a dozen in active use: SGD with Momentum, Nesterov accelerated gradient, Adagrad, Adadelta, RMSprop, AdaMax, Nadam, AMSGrad, and AdamW each address a limitation of earlier methods.

\citeauthor{ruder2016overview}'s 2016 overview article (\citeyear{ruder2016overview}) is the canonical practitioner survey of the family, with derivations of each rule and a discussion of which to reach for when.
A constant that cancels out (say, an additive constant in the loss) changes neither the gradients nor the model.
statements.section: Why a Hyperparameter Is Not a Constant

statements.quote: A hyperparameter does both:
statements.section: Why a Hyperparameter Is Not a Constant

statements.quote: * **Architecture hyperparameters change the model itself.** $d_{\text{model}} = 768$ and $d_{\text{model}} = 128$ are not two settings of the same model; they are two different function classes with different weight-matrix shapes.
statements.section: Why a Hyperparameter Is Not a Constant

statements.quote: Choosing $d_{\text{model}}$ is the choice of *which* set of functions the optimizer may search over.
statements.section: Why a Hyperparameter Is Not a Constant

statements.quote: * **Optimization hyperparameters change the process, not just its speed.** The learning rate does not merely pace the descent: gradient descent with a different step size follows a different trajectory and can settle in a different minimum.
statements.section: Why a Hyperparameter Is Not a Constant

statements.quote: Two runs that differ only in learning rate are different experiments, not one experiment at two speeds.
statements.section: Why a Hyperparameter Is Not a Constant

statements.quote: * **Data hyperparameters change the objective.** A different context length or a different tokenizer changes the loss the model is actually minimizing.
statements.section: Why a Hyperparameter Is Not a Constant

statements.quote: Consequence: there is no closed-form equation of the form $\text{hyperparameter} = f(\text{task})$ that you can solve.
statements.section: Why a Hyperparameter Is Not a Constant

statements.quote: The only way to know what a choice is worth is to run trainings and measure the result — or to fit a statistical model to the results of earlier runs.
statements.section: Why a Hyperparameter Is Not a Constant

statements.quote: **Evaluation is expensive.** One point in the search space costs one full training run.
At real scale that means days on thousands of GPUs; even a small model on one GPU costs minutes per point.
**The objective is noisy.** Two runs with the same hyperparameters but different random seeds land at slightly different losses.
A search must average over noise or it optimizes luck.

**The space is mixed and constrained.** Discrete values ($N$, $h$), continuous values (learning rate, best explored on a log scale), categorical choices (optimizer), plus constraints such as $d_{\text{model}} \bmod h = 0$.
A method that only handles one of these cannot handle the whole space.

**Hyperparameters interact.** Learning rate and batch size must be chosen together: doubling the batch size usually requires rescaling the learning rate — the linear scaling rule doubles it, up to a limit \cite{goyal2017largebatch}.
The search space is not a grid of independent dials.
Most published models ship with a hyperparameter table whose values were inherited from the previous model with a few adjustments.

Transfer works because architectures and objectives change slowly between papers — and it fails silently when the task or scale changes, because nothing tells you the inherited value is no longer good.
Before search became automatic, tuning was a craft with a short list of rules.

\cite[Bengio (2012)]{bengio2012practical} codified them for deep networks: the initial learning rate is “often the single most important hyperparameter” and should be tuned on a log scale; the batch size is mostly a computational choice; and random search is preferable to grid search when only a few axes matter.
The advice sounds modest, but it encodes the empirical fact that one hyperparameter dominates the others, which is why even a large Bayesian search usually starts by mapping that axis.
At the frontier, search is partly replaced by *fitted laws*.

(\cite[Kaplan et al., 2020]{kaplan2020scaling}) showed that the loss of a language model depends on the number of parameters $N$, the number of training tokens $D$ and the compute $C$ as smooth power laws.
Fit the laws on cheap small models and you can extrapolate the target size for a fixed budget.

(\cite[Hoffmann et al., 2022]{hoffmann2022chinchilla}) redid the analysis on a larger scale and found that for a fixed compute budget, models should be trained on roughly 20 times as many tokens as they have parameters — far more than the then-standard practice, which had been copied between papers for years.
A fitted law can thus overturn a prior belief that no single experiment would have questioned.
Scaling laws changed what search is for.

If the loss follows a power law in parameters and tokens, a handful of small runs can predict the compute-optimal frontier, and some hyperparameters can be transferred rather than re-searched at every scale.

\cite[Yang et al. (2022)]{yang2022mup} made this concrete with maximal-update parametrization (muP): many optimal hyperparameters — including the learning rate — stay stable as the model grows, so tuning a small model can be reused zero-shot on a large one.
The practical consequence is a shift from per-model search to a few scaled reference runs.
The simplest systematic method: choose a grid of candidate values per hyperparameter and train on every combination.

With $n$ points on each of $d$ axes this costs $n^d$ trainings, which grows so fast that grid search is only affordable for $d \approx 2$–3 — and it wastes budget on combinations where the unimportant axes are varied pointlessly.
Draw configurations at random (uniformly for discrete values, log-uniformly for positive continuous ones like the learning rate) and train on them.

(\cite[Bergstra & Bengio, 2012]{bergstra2010random}) showed that for a fixed evaluation budget, random search matches or beats grid search in most realistic settings: when only a few hyperparameters matter much, a grid spreads its points across the values of the ones that do not, while random search keeps covering the full range of every axis.

Build a probabilistic *surrogate model* of $\text{config} \mapsto \text{loss}$ from the evaluations already performed, and choose the next configuration by balancing **exploitation** (where the surrogate predicts a good loss) against **exploration** (where it is still uncertain).
Two standard instantiations:

* **Gaussian-process surrogates** — the classical form, introduced by \cite[Močkus (1975)]{mockus1978bo} and made practical for ML by \cite[Snoek et al. (2012)]{snoek2012practical}: a Gaussian process is placed over the loss function; an acquisition function (e.g. expected improvement) picks the next point from the balance of predicted quality and uncertainty.

* **TPE (Tree-structured Parzen Estimators)** — introduced by \cite[Bergstra et al. (2011)]{bergstra2011algorithms} and applied at scale by \cite[Bergstra et al. (2013)]{bergstra2013science}: instead of a full process, the observed configurations are split into those that gave a *good* loss and those that gave a *bad* one; each group is modeled by its own density, and the next configuration is sampled where the good density is high relative to the bad one.
Bayesian optimization treats the search as a sequential decision problem: maintain a belief about the objective, choose the point that maximizes expected improvement, observe, update.

\cite[Močkus (1975)]{mockus1978bo} gave the Bayesian formulation; \cite[Jones et al. (1998)]{jones1998ego} made Gaussian-process surrogates and expected improvement practical under the name “efficient global optimization”; \cite[Snoek et al. (2012)]{snoek2012practical} then adapted the machinery to ML models — a CIFAR-10 convolutional network, online LDA, and a structured SVM — and to the cost of each run.
The modern tooling descends from that line.
\cite[Hyperopt]{hyperopt} is the open-source implementation that popularised TPE; \cite[Optuna]{akiba2019optuna} and \cite[Ax]{olson2025ax} are the modern alternatives.
The defining property of the whole approach: *every evaluation makes the next one smarter*, so the search is sequential and budget-aware rather than exhaustive.
\cite[Li et al. (2016)]{li2016hyperband} turned this observation into an algorithm.

Hyperband runs successive-halving brackets: start many configurations with a tiny budget, keep the best fraction, and multiply the survivors' budget; a bracket repeats this until one configuration remains.

Running several brackets at different aggressiveness levels makes the method robust to the unknown cost of a full training run, and the whole procedure is a bandit-style allocation of trials rather than a surrogate model.
It remains the reference point for modern multi-fidelity schedulers.
\cite[Jaderberg et al. (2017)]{jaderberg2017pbt} pushed the idea further with population-based training.

A population of workers trains in parallel; at intervals, poorly performing workers copy the weights and hyperparameters of better ones and then perturb them, so the hyperparameters are *evolved* during training rather than fixed beforehand.

The method was demonstrated on deep reinforcement learning, machine translation and GANs — settings where schedules and exploration constants matter and runs are long — but it applies whenever a training run can be paused and forked.
It is search and training in one loop.
A bad configuration usually announces itself early: the loss curves of doomed runs separate from the survivors within the first few epochs.
Multi-fidelity methods therefore run many trials briefly and extend only the ones that are winning, so a fixed budget buys far more distinct configurations than running each trial to completion.
If you have a model whose training can be run as a program, the search does not have to be done by hand.
statements.section: A Tool for the Search: OmniOpt

statements.quote: \cite[ScaDS.AI Dresden/Leipzig]{omniopt} has developed exactly such an instrument: **OmniOpt**, a hyperparameter optimization tool that wraps an optimizer around your own program.
statements.section: A Tool for the Search: OmniOpt

statements.quote: Its current version, OmniOpt2, no longer ties the search to a single algorithm: it is built on the \cite[Ax]{olson2025ax} adaptive-experimentation platform, whose default surrogate is a Gaussian process fitted by \cite[BoTorch]{balandat2020botorch}, and it can additionally run TPE, Sobol quasi-random sequences, factorial designs, and the full range of \cite[Optuna]{akiba2019optuna} samplers.
statements.section: A Tool for the Search: OmniOpt

statements.quote: Which algorithm fits the problem is up to the search space: Gaussian processes shine in low-to-medium-dimensional continuous spaces, TPE in high-dimensional or heavily categorical ones, and quasi-random sequences when the evaluations are cheap enough that adaptivity pays no dividend.
statements.section: A Tool for the Search: OmniOpt

statements.quote: * Your program is a **black box** in any programming language on Linux: it reads the hyperparameters as command-line arguments, trains, and prints the objective value to standard output.
statements.section: A Tool for the Search: OmniOpt

statements.quote: * OmniOpt proposes the next configurations, balancing exploration and exploitation, and checks and installs all dependencies automatically.
statements.section: A Tool for the Search: OmniOpt

statements.quote: * The evaluations are distributed automatically over the HPC system at TU Dresden, given you have access to the system — more than 40,000 CPUs and several hundred GPUs.
statements.section: A Tool for the Search: OmniOpt

statements.quote: If you don't have access to the TU Dresden HPC systems, you can run it on any Linux, or any system that has Slurm as a scheduler.
statements.section: A Tool for the Search: OmniOpt

statements.quote: * The results come back as the full table of evaluated configurations plus 2D slices of the search space as color maps and parallel-coordinate plots.
statements.section: A Tool for the Search: OmniOpt
